exits.failMessage: A crystalline arch hums faintly. The transit link is dormant — you haven't attuned to this place yet.
A passage descends into deeper crystal. The way is sealed — the convergence has not been called. Yet.

lines: The Underlumen Threshold. You stand at the edge of the planet's living core.

The walls here are more crystal than stone. Veins of bioluminescent matter pulse in slow, rhythmic waves — not just glowing, but communicating. Patterns flow through the crystalline network like thoughts through neurons.
The air itself hums. Not sound — vibration. The entire chamber resonates with a frequency older than human civilization. The planet is aware of you.

The Underlumen has linked this place to the surface. A shortcut home.

Sable kneels at the edge of the crystal floor, one hand pressed flat against the stone. Her eyes are closed. When she speaks, her voice is barely a whisper.
'My grandmother told me about this place. She called it the Listening Floor. She said if you're still enough, you can hear the planet thinking.'

'The Underlumen isn't hostile. It's not trying to consume us or replace us. It's been here for millions of years, running the planet's systems — water cycles, mineral distribution, thermal regulation. It's infrastructure. Like the Array, but alive.'
'The Lighthouses suppress it. Push it deeper. The Array designed them that way — not to protect us from the dark, but to protect the Array from competition.'
'If we can prove this to the Council — that the Underlumen and biology can coexist, that they must coexist — we change everything.'
Sable doesn't look up from the crystal floor.
'We're here. The Listening Floor. My grandmother's stories were real.'
'The Underlumen runs everything beneath the surface. Water, minerals, heat. The Array suppresses it with the Lighthouses. That's the truth no one wanted to hear.'
'Get what Asha needs and go. The planet will decide what happens next, not us.'
The Threshold Keeper collapses, its crystalline shell fracturing into luminous shards. For a moment, the chamber dims — as if the Underlumen itself mourns.
Then the light returns, brighter than before. The veins in the walls pulse faster. Something noticed.
You press both hands against the crystalline floor. The vibration intensifies — not painful, but overwhelming. The boundary between you and the stone dissolves.
You see the planet. All of it. A network of crystal veins stretching from pole to pole, threading through bedrock and ocean floor. A nervous system for a world. The Underlumen.
It has been here for two hundred million years. It regulated the climate, distributed minerals, maintained the water table. It was the planet's immune system, its circulatory system, its memory.
Then the Array came. The Lighthouses drove it deep. Suppressed it. Not destroyed — the Array couldn't destroy it. But silenced. Contained. Made to sleep.
Now it's waking. And it doesn't want revenge. It wants what it always wanted: symbiosis. Partnership. Living systems working together.
The vision fades. You're kneeling on cold crystal, shaking. But you understand now. The three paths ahead aren't just political choices. They're biological ones.
With the Threshold Keeper gone, the chamber has changed. The crystal veins pulse freely now — no guardian to regulate the flow.
The bioluminescence is stronger. Warmer. Patterns emerge in the light: spirals, fractals, wave forms. The Underlumen is communicating.
Not to you specifically. To everything. To the stone, the water, the air. To the organisms that live in symbiosis with it. It's running diagnostics on a planetary scale.

The deeper you push into the chamber, the more the crystal patterns change. Near the entrance, the formations were branching veins — natural geometry. Here they're different.
Ordered. The luminescent pulses run in sequences that repeat, vary, repeat again in a different arrangement. Not geology. Not chemistry.
The Underlumen is running computations. And the variables it's working with — the patterns it's testing — look disturbingly like language.

A smooth crystal disc, worn to perfect flatness on one side by generations of hands. Unbounded in craft, ancient in material — the crystal predates human presence on Erith by millions of years. The Underlumen grew this long before there were people to hold it.
On the back, in archaic Unbounded script: a name you can't fully parse, and below it — 'She listened first. She heard the answer.'
This was left here deliberately. Someone from Sable's lineage made the descent, found this place, and left something behind to mark it. They came back. Someone always came back.
You press your hands against the crystal floor again. This time the response is immediate — directed. The Underlumen recognizes you.
The vibration focuses into a point beneath your palms. A formation rises slowly from the crystalline substrate: geometric, perfect, grown rather than built.
An 8x8 lattice of pre-human crystal — a Sol Unit frame assembled by a network that has been running planetary systems for two hundred million years. It was waiting for someone who understood.
The Underlumen Nexus. Not found. Given.
The Nexus settles into your grip — warm, resonant, alive in a way no manufactured device has ever been. Its crystalline substrate pulses in sync with your heartbeat.
8x8 grid. 15% cooldown reduction on everything. The planet itself gave you this.
You understand now that the Underlumen doesn't distinguish between its living and its tools. Both are part of the network. Both serve the system. Both endure.
